title: The United States Is Not Ready for the Arctic Age
gist: Reviewing Rana Foroohar's 'Sea Change,' Bobby Ghosh argues the U.S. is badly outmatched in the opening Arctic economy—three icebreakers versus Russia's 40-plus—because decades of offshoring hollowed out shipbuilding, leaving Washington dependent on Canada and Finland even as Trump antagonizes Ottawa with tariffs. The review endorses Foroohar's 'national security lives downstream from industrial capacity' thesis but flags the risks of tariffs and subsidies entrenching inefficiency.

insights.claim: The Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the planet, opening access to shipping lanes, fish stocks, energy, minerals and seafloor routes for communications cables.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Creates a new frontier for shipping, resource extraction and subsea-cable infrastructure investment.
insights.quote: The Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the planet
insights.locator: Rana Foroohar’s new book, Sea Change

insights.claim: The Arctic economic opportunity runs to at least hundreds of billions of dollars, and the late Guggenheim Partners CIO Scott Minerd saw potential for $1 trillion in infrastructure investment alone.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Sizes a multi-decade infrastructure and resource capex opportunity in the high north.
insights.quote: the late Scott Minerd, chief investment officer of Guggenheim Partners, saw potential for $1 trillion in investments in infrastructure alone.
insights.locator: Rana Foroohar’s new book, Sea Change

insights.claim: The post-Cold War era of 'Arctic exceptionalism,' when disputes were mediated and adversaries cooperated in science and shipping, has ended as an expansionist Russia, an ambitious China and a flailing United States bring great-power competition to the region.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Raises geopolitical risk premia for Arctic shipping and resource projects and supports polar defense spending.

insights.claim: Russia operates more than 40 icebreakers, many nuclear powered, China at least five, Canada's Coast Guard nine, while the U.S. Coast Guard has only three.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Quantifies a large U.S. capability deficit that will drive sustained icebreaker procurement spending.
insights.quote: Russia has more than 40 icebreakers, many of them nuclear powered, operating in the northern seas

insights.claim: The USCGC Healy is the only purpose-built, Arctic-ready U.S. icebreaker in regular service, and fires in 2020 and 2024 plus a mechanical failure in July left long spells with no U.S. icebreaker in the Arctic.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: U.S. Arctic presence is fragile and depends on allies until new vessels arrive years from now.

insights.claim: Trump ordered 11 icebreakers via no-bid contracts, but they will be built by a Finnish shipbuilder owned by a British company with Canadian roots, and only three by Gulf Copper in Galveston, Texas, with Finnish expertise.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: U.S. naval self-reliance rhetoric masks dependence on allied shipbuilders, benefiting Nordic and allied yards.
insights.locator: Trump is aware of the economic

insights.claim: In the Arctic, power stems from knowing the water and being able to move through it, so icebreakers are the cornerstone of economic, scientific and military activity there.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Icebreaker fleet size is a useful proxy for national competitiveness in Arctic resource and shipping access.
insights.quote: In the Arctic, power stems from knowing the water and being able to move through it.

insights.claim: Despite Trump's claim that 'we don't need Canada,' the U.S. imports about 4 million barrels a day of crude oil from Canada plus electricity, aluminum and auto parts.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Tariffs on Canadian exports hit critical U.S. energy and industrial inputs, raising costs for U.S. refiners and manufacturers.
insights.quote: the United States depends a great deal on Canada, to the tune of 4 million barrels of crude oil a day, plus electricity, aluminum, auto parts, and much else besides.

insights.claim: U.S. prospects in the Arctic depend on close cooperation with Canada, making Trump's fresh tariffs on Canadian exports an extraordinary act of self-harm.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: U.S.-Canada trade friction undermines joint Arctic strategy and the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort.
insights.locator: Viewed from the vicinity of the North Pole

insights.claim: At the end of World War II U.S. shipyards produced more than half the world's commercial tonnage, but today the U.S. builds fewer than five commercial ships a year while naval construction suffers delays, cost overruns and labor shortages.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Underpins the case for sustained U.S. industrial-policy support for shipbuilding and naval suppliers.
insights.quote: Today, the country builds fewer than five commercial ships a year, while naval construction suffers delays, cost overruns, and labor shortages.

insights.claim: Foroohar argues that national security lives downstream from industrial capacity, updating Alfred Thayer Mahan's sea-power thesis for an age of industrial policy.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Supports a durable policy regime favoring onshoring of strategic industries like shipbuilding and defense.
insights.quote: national security lives downstream from industrial capacity.
insights.locator: This is perilous, not only for U.S.

insights.claim: U.S. shipbuilding decayed because policy and Wall Street treated the lowest immediate price as the highest good, offshoring production and shedding inventory and redundant suppliers as waste.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Reversal of efficiency-first logic implies higher input costs but more resilient supply chains for strategic sectors.

insights.claim: A balance sheet can record savings from buying a cheaper foreign-built ship but not the loss of knowing how to build one, and a supply chain cannot be quickly recreated once it has disappeared.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Lost industrial know-how means rebuilding shipbuilding capacity will be slow and costly, extending reliance on allied yards.
insights.quote: A balance sheet can trace the savings made and profits accrued from buying a cheaper, foreign-built ship, but it can’t register the loss of knowing how to build one.

insights.claim: The Biden administration began using industrial policy to rebuild strategic industries, including signing the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort with Canada and Finland.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Trilateral icebreaker cooperation is the main channel for near-term U.S. Arctic capability.

insights.claim: Tariffs can preserve an industry but also its inefficiencies, and government support can become a permanent subsidy to politically connected companies, so the U.S. needs better ways to decide which goods are truly essential and how much extra to pay.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Flags crony-capitalism and inefficiency risk in protected U.S. industrial-policy beneficiaries.
insights.quote: Tariffs can preserve an industry, but they can also preserve its inefficiencies.
